newsitem.title: USA: US ethanol tax-credit loss would force diversity.
newsitem.headline: US ethanol tax-credit loss would force diversity.

text.p: If U.S. ethanol plants are to survive after the year 2000, when a federal tax break on ethanol expires, improved efficiency and production diversity will be needed, ethanol industry sources said.

Although some attendees at the Renewable Fuels Association conference here were optimistic the U.S. Congress can be convinced to extend the tax break beyond 2000, others are not confident of an extension and said the industry must become more efficient.
"We have got to continue to work to get costs down," said Frank Moore, general manager of Heartland Grain Fuels, L.P.
Moore said technological advances are needed over the next three years to cut production costs to maintain ethanol as a cost-effective fuel additive.

Heartland Grain Fuels produces about eight million gallons of ethanol annually, but is developing other products that could help the company survive should the ethanol tax break expire in three years.

Heartland and other ethanol producers rely on 5.6-cent per gallon excise tax exemption to make ethanol competitive with other oxygenate fuel additives. These additives, when mixed with gasoline, reduce harmful automobile emissions.
"If they were to end the tax incentive tomorrow every ethanol plant would die," Moore said.

Archer Daniels Midland Co, Decatur, Ill., the largest producer of ethanol, is converting some of its ethanol capacity to make beverage and industrial alcohol, ADM senior vice president Martin Andreas told Reuters during the conference.

Many ethanol producers are not ready to admit defeat on the tax issue. They remain optimistic that by promoting ethanol's economic and environmental benefits the U.S. Congress can be convinced to extend the tax credit beyond 2000.
"This industry is providing too many benefits," said Neil Koehler, a partner in Parallel Products, a California ethanol producer, referring to the pending loss of the tax break.
But at the very least, uncertainty about the future of the tax break is taking a toll.
"Obviously it puts a damper on expansion plans," Koehler said.

There are 50 ethanol plants in 19 states which can produce about 1.5 billion gallons annually, the RFA said. These plants process 560 million bushels of corn annually and contribute about six percent to the income of U.S. corn farmers.
